chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdullah, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Khalid ibn Najih, from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), who said:
When you see a man who has been afflicted, and Allah has favored you, then say: 'O Allah, I am neither ridiculing nor priding myself, but I am praising You for the great bounty of Yours upon me.'
ai.seo_question: What should a Muslim say when seeing someone in need while they are blessed?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi emphasizes the spiritual discipline of maintaining humility during moments of comparative advantage, specifically instructing the believer to distinguish between mere lack of arrogance and active gratitude. It highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on internalizing thankfulness (shukr) as a safeguard against the subtle corruption of pride when witnessing others' trials. The supplication serves as a practical tool for converting social observation into a moment of divine connection and self-reflection.

en.hubeali:
A number of our companions, from Ahmad Bin Abu Abdullah, from Usman Bin Isa, from Khalid Bin Najeeh, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:

‘When you see the man who has been afflicted and Allah<sup>azwj</sup> has Favoured upon you, so say, ‘O Allah<sup>azwj</sup>! I am neither ridiculing nor priding, but I am praising You<sup>azwj</sup> upon the great Bounty of Yours<sup>azwj</sup> upon me’.
en.sarwar: 22. A number of our people have narrated from Ahmad ibn ‘Abd Allah from ‘Uthman ibn ‘Isa from Khalid ibn Najih from abu ‘Abd Allah (a.s.) who has said the following: “Abu ‘Abd Allah (a.s.) has said, ‘
When you see a man who is in affliction and Allah has granted you a favor, say, “O Allah, I do not ridicule him or boast, but I express Your praise for the great favors that You have done for me.”’”
